newsitem.title: IRAN: U.S. should release frozen Iran assets - paper.
newsitem.headline: U.S. should release frozen Iran assets - paper.

text.p: Washington should release Iran's frozen assets in the United States, held since the 1979 U.S. embassy hostage crisis, as a positive overture for better relations, an Iranian newspaper said on Thursday.
The United States froze billions of dollars in Iranian assets held in U.S. banks after militant Islamist students stormed the embassy in Tehran in November 1979 and took its staff hostage.
They demanded extradition of the U.S.-backed Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, who had been overthrown in a revolution led by Shi'ite Moslem clergymen earlier that year.
Fifty-two Americans were to be held for 444 days in a crisis which poisoned relations between the two former allies.

Tehran Times daily, calling for the United States to take the initiative to improve relations, said the major outcome of the Islamic revolution was the independence of the Iranian nation "which, the U.S. fears, may set the example to the people in the countries under its domination".
Iran's president-elect Mohammad Khatami, voted into office last Friday and due to take over in August, said on Tuesday Washington held the key to any thaw in relations with Tehran.

"Thus, any change in Iran's U.S. policy depends on the U.S. renouncing its smear campaign, rectifying its hostile stance against Iran and redressing its past mistakes," Tehran Times said. "A positive overture could be the release of Iran's frozen assets in the United States."

U.S. officials have said repeatedly there can be no improvement in relations until Iran renounces involvement in international "terrorism", halts attempts to acquire nuclear and other weapons of mass destruction, and stops trying to wreck the Middle East peace process.

U.S. analysts in Washington have described Khatami's landslide election as a turning point in the revolution and said the United States should respond with new overtures to show it is serious about its oft-stated readiness to open a new dialogue.
